Title: California warns of measles exposure in six counties from unvaccinated train passenger
Article_Text:
California public health officials are warning of a possible measles exposure spanning multiple counties after an infected and unvaccinated passenger traveled through the state via Amtrak trains and thruway buses.
The warning comes as the US faces its largest measles resurgence in more than three decades, fueled largely by growing vaccine hesitancy.
The California department of public health said the traveler passed through at least six counties – Alameda, Butte, Kern, Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Joaquin – while making multiple transfers.
Officials said the passenger entered California on an Amtrak train that arrived in Los Angeles on 10 September. From there, the traveler continued to Bakersfield before heading through Stockton, Oroville, Sacramento and Emeryville, eventually leaving California for Denver.
Health officials said passengers who were onboard the same trains or buses, as well as people who were inside the stations along the route on the dates involved, have been exposed to measles.
The state said it is working with federal partners and local health departments to identify and notify people who may have been exposed.
“This case, along with previous measles outbreaks in California this year, serve as reminders of the importance of vaccination against measles,” assistant state public health officer Rita Nguyen said in a statement. “The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is safe and provides long-lasting protection against measles. Vaccination protects both our own families and those who are too young to be fully vaccinated.”
Pennsylvania is currently dealing with the country’s worst active measles outbreak. The Pennsylvania health department announced on Wednesday that 731 cases have been confirmed across 38 counties so far this year. At least four people in the state have died from measles-related illness.
Pennsylvania is now seeking emergency assistance from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as the outbreak continues to spread. State officials have warned, however, that the request could be withdrawn unless the CDC publicly recognizes the four measles-associated deaths, something the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, previously instructed the CDC not to do.
And as the death toll from the outbreak continues to rise, Kennedy headlined the Washington DC conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense earlier this week, an group he led for nearly a decade.
He only addressed the measles outbreak in Pennsylvania once during his speech, instead peddling unfounded fears about vaccines at a time when health experts are urgently encouraging people to vaccinate against measles.
“In our country we care about rare illnesses and deaths. We care about every child who dies from measles. They get headlines,” he said. “I’d ask you to care about children who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries.”
The California warning also follows another recent mass-exposure incident involving Amtrak.
Earlier this week, it was reported that a person infected with measles traveled onboard an Amtrak train from Sedalia, Missouri, to Chicago, Illinois, resulting in more than 250 people being exposed to the virus in Jackson county alone.
This month, it was also revealed that the Trump administration changed how measles deaths are counted during the outbreak. The CDC is now relying on data from the National Center for Health Statistics, which is used to track mortality trends over time. It is unclear why this change was made.

Title: Illegal Alien Pleads Guilty in Grandparent Scam Money Laundering Case, Faces Up to 20 Years
Article_Text:
A Dominican Republic resident illegally living in Perth Amboy, New Jersey, pleaded guilty in federal court to a charge of money laundering conspiracy in connection with a grandparent fraud scheme, United States Attorney Troy Rivetti announced today.
Advertisement
Elvys Nicanor Nunez Valerio, 33, pleaded guilty to one count before Senior United States District Judge Nora Barry Fischer on September 14, 2026.
In connection with the guilty plea, the Court was advised that Valerio was a participant in a sophisticated grandparent fraud scheme operating out of the Dominican Republic in which an organized crime group impersonating a grandchild — or other close relative — in a crisis contacted elderly victims and asked for immediate financial assistance. The scammers arranged for a rideshare driver to pick up cash from the elderly relative and deliver the money to a member of the criminal group. From there, portions of the money were deposited into bank accounts or sent back to the Dominican Republic via money transfer services. Specifically, Valerio’s role in the conspiracy was to receive the fraud proceeds from the rideshare drivers, to further launder the money, and ultimately to transfer the money to the Dominican Republic.
On July 12, 2025, an elderly resident of the Western District of Pennsylvania was contacted as part of the grandparent scheme and was deceived into providing $10,000 to a rideshare driver who came to his home to pick up the funds. Subsequently, the victim’s family learned of the fraud and contacted the Pennsylvania State Police. The victim was still in contact with the scammer, who instructed the victim to pay another $12,000 so that his daughter could be released from prison. A driver picked up the second package, which did not contain any fraud proceeds. The Pennsylvania State Police initiated a traffic stop on the rideshare driver, who was an unknowing participant in the fraud. Authorities then allowed the driver to deliver the package to its destination address in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. The driver provided the second package to Valerio, who was stopped by the Pennsylvania State Police before he was able to drive away.
Recommended
A search of the vehicle resulted in the recovery of the second package as well as fraud proceeds associated with the first package. Further investigation revealed that Valerio was involved in the larger conspiracy and had traveled around the country participating in the fraud. Activity in a bank account in Valerio’s name was determined to be consistent with involvement in the scheme, including, between January and July 2025, more than 40 cash deposits totaling more than $65,000. The financial records also showed payments to and from other members of the conspiracy and transfers of the fraud proceeds to the Dominican Republic.
Judge Fischer scheduled sentencing for December 1, 2026. The law provides for a total sentence of up to 20 years in prison, a fine of up to $500,000, or both. Under the federal Sentencing Guidelines, the actual sentence imposed is based upon the seriousness of the offense and the prior criminal history, if any, of the defendant.
Two of Valerio’s co-conspirators, Luis Alfonso Bisono Rodriguez and Engels Guillermo Almengot Valerio, both also of the Dominican Republic and illegally residing in the U.S., each were sentenced by Judge Fischer earlier this month to two years of prison, to be followed by three years of supervised release, on their convictions for money laundering conspiracy in relation to the grandparent fraud scheme.
Assistant United States Attorney Brendan T. Conway is prosecuting this case on behalf of the government.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation and Pennsylvania State Police, in conjunction with numerous other police departments throughout the United States, conducted the investigation that led to the prosecution of Valerio.

Title: Hitting the Right Note: Nittany Valley Symphony Celebrates Diamond Anniversary
Article_Text:
This story originally appeared in the September 2026 issue of Town&Gown magazine.
When her son began learning how to play the violin, Avis Jones remembered the viola she played in high school. She enjoyed playing the instrument, although only for a year.
“My husband surprised me with viola lessons,” Jones says.
In her mid-30s, she took lessons — relearning the basics and remembering the joy of playing music. Those lessons and a conversation with a founding member have led to 40 years of playing her viola in the Nittany Valley Symphony.
“I stuck with it and made some of my best friends,” she says.
Jones is one of many members who have come together to make music for 60 years in the Centre Region.
The Nittany Valley Symphony began as a small but mighty group organized by Ann Keller, who wanted to perform concerts in the schools and community to grow music in the area. She organized a symphonic performance at the first Central Pennsylvania Festival of the Arts.
“It was originally created so people who aren’t professional musicians had a place and community to play with,” says executive director, Rebecca Richards. “We are still a community orchestra.”
Today, the symphony includes 60 to 80 members. Some players are paid, while others volunteer their time and talent. Most are from Centre County and have full-time careers in other fields. They come together for the love of music, rehearsing as a group six or seven times before performing for the community.
The Nittany Valley Symphony has been a community for Jones and extension of her family over the past four decades. Although initially nervous, Jones continued attending rehearsals. She grew her love of music and friendships, both of which proved to be lifelong.
“I think one of the nicest things is to be this age and have close friends who are my age and older, and as young as their 20s,” says Jones, who will celebrate her 80th birthday this month.
Two years into playing with the group, Jones was elected president of the symphony. With community and volunteer support, she led efforts to become a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, establish a board of directors, form committees, fundraise for future seasons, create advertising, and sell tickets.
The group brought in a paid conductor and continued to grow.
“They help you shape every single note, piece, and phrase,” she says of the conductors.
Current conductor and musical director Timothy Farrand officially began his tenure in 2023. Farrand earned a master’s degree in conducting and has been active in the State College music community. The symphony invited him to guest conduct two concerts in 2022 after the passing of Michael Jinbo, who served as conductor and director for 32 years.
“The Nittany Valley Symphony has been a wonderful organization to work with musically and collaboratively, with a bunch of wonderful human beings,” Farrand says.
In preparation for its 60th season, Farrand went through the Nittany Valley Symphony’s archives to select pieces from the group’s history. The performances flow throughout the season, varying from pops to chamber and classical music pieces.
The anniversary season will culminate in April 2027 with “Dreamers and Visionaries: 60th Anniversary Celebration” at the Penn State Eisenhower Auditorium.
“The most rewarding element is to see it come to fruition,” he says. “Each musician puts their own touch on the music and their personalities shine through. The process is incredibly rewarding.”
Honoring the symphony’s history while connecting with audience members is important to Farrand.
“Music is tapping into these stories of every facet of our human experience,” Farrand says.
Compositions from Beethoven and Dvorak investigate the peaks and valleys of humanity.
“It’s a deeply personal experience for every single person — and it’s their own experience.”
Richards, Farrand, and Jones each expressed gratitude for the part the Nittany Valley Symphony has played in their lives. They hope the group will continue to play for years to come.
“It’s very exciting to do all this preparation to perform and have people enjoying what you’re producing,” Jones says. “It’s wonderful that we’re still around after 60 years.”
Jones encouraged the community to check out one of the upcoming performances.
“You don’t realize how much you love classical music because you haven’t sat and listened,” she says. “Come to a concert, close your eyes and let your emotions go. See what you feel. Music brings out all the feelings you have that words are not powerful enough to convey.”
The Nittany Valley Symphony and its members perform in a variety of venues around the Centre Region. It will open its 2026-27 season with “Dreams of the Forest” at 3 p.m. Sunday, Sept. 20, at Bellefonte Area High School.
Learn more about the Nittany Valley Symphony and check out its 60th anniversary season online at nvs.org. T&G
Hannah Pollock is a writer, photographer, and retired string instrument player who was inspired by this story to take her violin out of its case.

Title: Ed Sheeran Defended by Former Opening Act Aaron Rowe, Irish Singer Reveals Real Person to Blame
Article_Text:
Ed Sheeran Defended by Former Opening Act Aaron Rowe, Irish Singer Reveals Real Person to Blame
Aaron Rowe is coming to Ed Sheeran‘s defense after exiting the Loop Tour.
Earlier this week, the Irish singer-songwriter announced that he was dropping out as one of the opening acts of the 35-year-old “Shape of You” singer’s tour in solidarity with Macklemore and Palestine. Every other opening act, along with Ed‘s band, then followed suit and also dropped out.
In a new video posted to Instagram on Friday (September 18), Aaron spoke out in support of Ed and said that people are focusing on the wrong person and issue. Instead, Aaron said that billionaire New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft is the real person to blame in this situation.
“I’m gonna be honest. I think you are all focusing on the wrong person here,” Aaron said. “All I keep hearing is Ed Sheeran this, Ed Sheeran that — when you really should be focusing on the likes of Robert Kraft. You really should be focusing on the Zionist lobbies that are trying to silence the voices of people who are shouting about genocide, the genocide that is happening in Palestine right now by Israel.”
Aaron then acknowledged that Ed‘s statement in the wake of the fallout “could have been a lot better.” After Macklemore revealed that he was removed from the tour, Ed said that it was not his decision, but that of tour promoter Messina Touring Group along with pressure from Kraft, 85, who banned the rapper from performing at his Gillette Stadium.
Aaron then reaffirmed that he does not think Macklemore should have been removed from the tour and thought the panic led to someone rushing a decision.
“I haven’t had a chance to f***ing talk to Ed too much, but I fully believe he knows that was a mistake,” he said, noting everyone on the lineup supported Palestinians living in Gaza.
“Like, if Ed Sheeran was a f***ing Zionist, why would he have all these f***ing people on the f***ing tour?” Aaron added.
He then said he believed that Ed knows he made a mistake and took his home country of Ireland, other governments, the media, and the music industry to task who he said have “done f*** all” about the situation, despite having “so much money and so much power that they’re able to basically shut down any opinion that they don’t agree with.”
“You should be using this opportunity to plaster Robert Kraft’s face everywhere, someone who tried to shut down free speech, someone who tried to silence the voices of people who are shouting out genocide,” Aaron asserted. “That’s what you should be using your energy on, not f***ing Ed Sheeran, for f***’s sake.”
Ed is scheduled to resume his Loop Tour on Saturday night, September 19 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia. He’s made a major change to the show after losing his opening acts.

Title: Telehealth companies keep exposing their customers' medical data. What should they do?
Article_Text:
Telehealth companies keep exposing their customers’ medical data. What should they do?
WASHINGTON (AP) — The appeal of telehealth is easy to explain: Instead of calling a doctor, booking an appointment and hoping to eventually get a prescription, you can log onto an app or website and get approved for a new medication within minutes.
Since the COVID-19 pandemic, scores of online health services have launched with the promise of quick, convenient access to drugs for ADHD, sexual dysfunction, anxiety, weight loss and more.
Increasingly, though, government regulators are accusing these companies of deceptive, unethical business practices, including disclosing their customers’ health data, signing them up for hard-to-cancel subscriptions and bypassing real-time consultations with doctors.
The Federal Trade Commission’s latest lawsuit alleges that telehealth pioneer Hims & Hers engaged in all of those tactics, running afoul of U.S. consumer protection laws.
Hims has disputed the government’s claims, calling them “an effort to generate headlines at our expense.”
In recent years, FTC officials have filed similar cases against more than a half-dozen telehealth companies, including online therapy provider BetterHelp and pharmacy discount service GoodRx. In both cases, regulators said the companies shared users’ health data with online platforms such as Meta and Google, without getting permission.
Experts say part of the problem is that federal laws that govern the handling of health information generally don’t apply to telehealth companies.
“There’s an entire universe of companies collecting huge amounts of consumer health data every day that aren’t covered by our current health sector-specific laws,” said Andrew Crawford, an attorney with the nonprofit Center for Democracy and Technology.
Here are some things to know before signing up for a telehealth service:
Don’t expect to actually talk to a physician
Nearly all telehealth visits begin with a questionnaire in which users provide details about their medical history and possible medications they’re interested in.
According to the FTC’s lawsuit, Hims customers were automatically enrolled and billed for recurring prescriptions with “virtually no opportunity to review the provider’s recommended treatment.”
Researchers have documented similar practices across the industry, even for injectable weight-loss drugs that typically require a physical exam and other precautions before beginning treatment.
A recent analysis of nearly 50 telehealth companies selling GLP-1 drugs found that less than a third actually required any real-time video or audio consultation with a physician. In some cases, the prescriptions were approved within minutes.
“What we saw overwhelmingly was that it was incredibly easy to get access to the GLP-1s,” said Dr. Reshma Ramachandran of Yale University, who led the study. “Most of the time, the prescription was automatically sent, without even an opportunity to stop the dispensing.”
The lack of a real-time conversation means many patients aren’t getting the type of care recommended by medical societies that prescribe GLP-1s, including discussions about weight-loss goals, past efforts and eating disorders.
Only a little more than half the websites had a question about eating disorders — which GLP-1 drugs can induce or worsen — on their intake questionnaires, the researchers found.
Your data may be shared with advertisers, social media companies and others
Americans often assume that any personal health information they share is protected by HIPAA, the federal privacy law that governs the handling of medical information. But the law generally only applies to specific types of health businesses, including medical offices, hospitals and insurers, not telehealth companies offering prescriptions, counseling, DNA tests and other online services.
Privacy experts say that legal gap is one reason companies continue to disclose sensitive health information to advertisers and search engines.
“There isn’t a clear federal law saying: ‘Don’t do this,’” said Justin Brookman, Consumer Reports’ director of technology policy. “There’s just a body of soft law and settled cases with the FTC that many companies probably aren’t even aware of.”
Because HIPAA does not cover every direct-to-consumer health platform, the FTC has generally used its broader authority to take action against “fraudulent, deceptive or unethical business methods.” In practice, that means showing that telehealth companies disclosed their customers’ health information after initially saying they wouldn’t.
Hims told customers that its platform offered a “100% online, private and secure” means of sharing information with the company’s medical professionals, according to the FTC complaint. But instead the company shared the data with Meta and other online platforms, the FTC alleges.
Still, experts say the penalties available to regulators are limited. In most cases, companies sign a legal agreement stating that they’ll stop the practices cited by regulators.
Lawmakers in California, Connecticut, Maryland and other states have passed new online privacy laws that include special protections for health information. But there’s been little enforcement against telehealth companies that break those rules.
Online privacy tools offer a bit of protection
For now, privacy experts recommend using ad blockers and private web browsers — sometimes called “incognito” windows — when logging onto telehealth websites. Those tools can make it harder for companies to track your location, online history and other personal information.
It’s also a good idea to read any user agreements to get a sense of how the company plans to use your personal data, said Crawford. Some telehealth sites, for example, explicitly state in their privacy policies that they have the right to sell data about users’ sex lives.
The only surefire way to protect your information may simply be to decline the terms of service, usually one of the first steps required before accessing telehealth.
